pos: n. (the fixed round of daily prayer and psalmody appointed in the monastic and Roman use)
etymology: Latin officium divinum, the divine duty or service; from opus, work, and facere, to do — a work owed.
biblical_def: The Divine Office is the appointed round of daily prayer, psalm and lesson which the monastic houses and the Roman church recited at fixed hours, from midnight to bedtime, the whole Psalter normally traversed within a week. Its materials are overwhelmingly biblical, and the instinct behind it is not foreign to Scripture. The Psalmist says “Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments” (Psa 119:164), and again “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud” (Psa 55:17); Daniel “kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime” (Dan 6:10); Peter and John went up to the temple “at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1). Fixed hours of prayer are therefore no invention of the cloister. What Scripture nowhere does is make the recitation itself a meritorious work, or bind a man's conscience to a quota of syllables. The Office became, in the later medieval centuries, an obligation discharged rather than a worship offered — said privately, at speed, in a tongue the sayer sometimes did not understand. The Reformers kept the goods and refused the yoke: Scripture read in course, the Psalter sung whole, morning and evening prayer in the language of the people, and no man's salvation hanging on it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines office as a particular duty, charge or trust, and also the forms of divine service; divine as pertaining to the true God; service as the act of serving, or performance of duty to God; and prayer as a solemn address to the Supreme Being.
webster_full: OFFICE, n. A particular duty, charge or trust conferred by public authority and for a public purpose; also, that which is performed, intended or assigned to be done by a particular person or thing.
OFFICE, n. In the Romish and Episcopal churches, the forms of divine service appointed to be used at particular times or on particular occasions; as the office for the dead.
DIVINE, a. Pertaining to the true God; as the divine nature; divine perfections.
SERVICE, n. The act of serving; the office of a servant; also, obedience; the performance of duty to God, in acts of worship.

PRAYER, n. In worship, a solemn address to the Supreme Being, consisting of adoration, or an expression of our sense of God's glorious perfections, confession of our sins, supplication for mercy and forgiveness, intercession for blessings on others, and thanksgiving.
scriptures: Seven times a day do I praise thee because of thy righteous judgments.
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.

Now when Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house; and his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime.
Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
corruption_summary: The fixed round of daily prayer: biblical in instinct, meritorious in later Roman practice, and now resold as a wellness rhythm with the God of it removed.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval corruption was to make the Office a work. A duty counted, timed and owed can be discharged without being meant, and Christ had already named the danger: “when ye pray, use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do: for they think that they shall be heard for their much speaking” (Mat 6:7). Paul put the same error under its proper heading when he wrote of practices that “have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body” (Col 2:23) — religion a man appoints for himself, however devout its hours.

The present corruption is stranger. The monastic hours have been lifted whole out of the faith that built them and sold back as a daily rhythm or personal rule for the exhausted professional — the structure kept because it is found to regulate attention, the God addressed quietly dropped. That is the Office emptied, not recovered. The principle to recover is that fixed hours are a scaffold for real address to a real God, never a technique for managing the self: “men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1).
roots_summary: Hebrew tephillah (H8605), prayer; Hebrew halal (H1984), to praise; Greek proseuche (G4335), prayer; Greek hora (G5610), an hour; Greek leitourgia (G3009), a public service.
roots_lines: Hebrew tephillah (H8605) — prayer, intercession; “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense” (Psa 141:2).
Hebrew halal (H1984) — to praise, to boast in; “Seven times a day do I praise thee” (Psa 119:164).
Greek proseuche (G4335) — prayer offered to God; “the hour of prayer” (Act 3:1).
Greek hora (G5610) — an hour, a fixed point of the day; “Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9).
Greek leitourgia (G3009) — a public service rendered; the word behind “liturgy”, service owed and offered.
usage: “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray” (Psa 55:17) — the three hours the Psalmist kept, long before a cloister kept them.
“use not vain repetitions, as the heathen do” (Mat 6:7) — the standing warning over every fixed form, Protestant forms included.
“Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17) — the command no timetable can discharge and none should be allowed to replace.

pos: n. pl. (the seven or eight fixed times of daily prayer appointed by church rule)
etymology: Greek kanon, a measuring rod or rule, through Latin canonicus, according to rule; with hora, an hour. Hours measured out by rule.
biblical_def: The canonical hours are the fixed times of prayer appointed by ecclesiastical rule: matins and lauds before dawn, prime at the first hour, terce at the third, sext at the sixth, none at the ninth, vespers at evening and compline at bedtime. The division is older than the monasteries that perfected it. Scripture itself marks the hours of prayer — “the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1), and Peter praying “about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9); the Psalmist keeps “Evening, and morning, and at noon” (Psa 55:17); and the night watches have their own office in “all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1). A Christian who sets times to pray is walking in a very old and very good path. What the word canonical added was obligation: these hours by rule, their omission a fault requiring confession, their recitation a debt to the church. That is where Scripture parts company with the system. The rule may order a house; it may not bind a conscience as though God had commanded it. Fixed hours are a servant of prayer and a tyrant the moment they are made its measure.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines canonical as pertaining to a canon, according to the ecclesiastical canons, and notes canonical hours as certain stated times of the day appropriated to prayer; and hour as the twenty-fourth part of a day.
webster_full: CANONICAL, a. Pertaining to a canon; according to the canon or rule.
CANONICAL HOURS, certain stated times of the day, fixed by ecclesiastical laws, or appropriated to the offices of prayer and devotion.
HOUR, n. A space of time equal to the twenty fourth part of the natural day; sixty minutes.
CANON, n. In ecclesiastical affairs, a law or rule of doctrine or discipline, enacted by a council and confirmed by the sovereign.
STATED, a. Settled; established; regular; occurring at regular times.
scriptures: Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.
A Song of degrees. Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD.
corruption_summary: Fixed times of prayer by church rule: a good scaffold turned into an obligation, and lately into a productivity schedule with the prayer taken out.
corruption_paragraphs: The historic corruption is the word canonical itself. Setting times to pray is wisdom; decreeing them under pain of sin is to legislate where God has not spoken, and Paul met the same spirit in men who would judge a brother by a calendar. Christ's own practice is instructive and free: “in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35) — an hour kept, not an hour owed.

The modern misuse keeps the grid and discards the Object. Fixed hours are now recommended for focus, circadian hygiene and the management of attention, and the recommendation is often sound as far as it goes; it simply is not prayer. The principle to recover is that an hour is holy because of who is addressed in it, not because of where it falls in the day: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee” (Psa 5:3).
roots_summary: Greek kanon (G2583), a rule; Greek hora (G5610), an hour; Hebrew eth (H6256), a set time; Hebrew tamid (H8548), continual; Greek kairos (G2540), a season.
roots_lines: Greek kanon (G2583) — a measuring rod, hence a rule or standard; the root of “canonical” and of “canon”.
Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1).
Hebrew eth (H6256) — a set or appointed time, the hour fixed for a thing.
Hebrew tamid (H8548) — continual, the word of the daily sacrifice morning and evening.
Greek kairos (G2540) — a season or opportune moment, time regarded by its fitness rather than its length.
usage: “Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9) — an apostle keeping an hour, with no rule compelling him.
“which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1) — the night office has a biblical warrant the obligation never had.
“From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD” (Psa 113:3) — the day bounded by praise rather than carved into debts.

pos: n. pl. (the dawn office of praise, following matins in the monastic and Roman use)
etymology: Latin laudes, praises, the plural of laus, praise; so named from the Laudate psalms with which the hour closes.
biblical_def: Lauds is the office of daybreak, following hard on the night office of matins and taking its name from the psalms of praise that end it. Of all the hours it is the one with the plainest biblical warrant, for Scripture ties praise to the morning again and again: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psa 5:3); “To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night” (Psa 92:2); “Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early” (Psa 57:8). The content of the hour was almost wholly Scripture — psalms, a canticle from the prophets, the Benedictus — and in that it was better than much that has replaced it. The defect was never the material but the framing: an hour rendered because the rule required it, in a Latin many of the brethren followed only by habit, and credited to the house as part of its service to God. Praise that is owed on a schedule may still be real praise; it may also become the form of thanksgiving without its substance. Scripture asks for the first and warns against the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines lauds as that part of divine service which immediately follows matins; laud as praise, or a hymn of praise; praise as the commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues; and morning as the first part of the day, beginning at twelve o'clock at night.
webster_full: LAUDS, n. In the Romish church, that part of divine service which immediately follows matins.
LAUD, n. Praise; commendation; honorable mention. Also, a hymn or song of praise.
LAUD, v.t. To praise; to celebrate or extol in words or song; to magnify.
PRAISE, n. Commendation bestowed on a person for his personal virtues or worthy actions; the expression of gratitude for personal favors conferred; a glorifying or extolling.
MORNING, n. The first part of the day, beginning at twelve o'clock at night and extending to twelve at noon; but in a more limited sense, the time from break of day to the hour of breakfast.
scriptures: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning, and thy faithfulness every night,
Awake up, my glory; awake, psaltery and harp: I myself will awake early.
From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD'S name is to be praised.
corruption_summary: The dawn office of praise: the most scriptural of the hours, and still vulnerable to praise recited as a duty owed rather than offered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that morning praise is the native speech of a redeemed man, not an institutional obligation. “From the rising of the sun unto the going down of the same the LORD” (Psa 113:3) — the Psalmist bounds his whole day with it, and nobody appointed him to do so.

The live temptation is the one Hebrews addresses by calling praise a sacrifice: “By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name” (Heb 13:15). A sacrifice costs; a recitation need not. Where lauds became the latter, the hour survived and the praise did not — and no Protestant morning service is immune to the same hollowing.
roots_summary: Hebrew halal (H1984), to praise; Hebrew todah (H8426), thanksgiving; Hebrew boqer (H1242), morning; Greek aineo (G134), to praise; Greek ainesis (G133), praise offered.
roots_lines: Hebrew halal (H1984) — to praise, to shine forth; the root of “hallelujah”.
Hebrew boqer (H1242) — morning, the breaking of light; “in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee” (Psa 5:3).
Hebrew todah (H8426) — thanksgiving, confession made in praise.
Greek ainesis (G133) — praise offered up; “the sacrifice of praise to God continually” (Heb 13:15).
Latin laudate — “praise ye”, the imperative that opens the psalms from which the hour is named.
usage: “I myself will awake early” (Psa 57:8) — the resolve that lauds was built to serve.
“To shew forth thy lovingkindness in the morning” (Psa 92:2) — the morning office stated in a single line.
“Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD” (Psa 150:6) — the breadth no single hour can contain.

pos: n. (the first of the little canonical hours, said at the first hour of daylight)
etymology: Latin prima hora, the first hour; from primus, first. The hour of the working day's beginning.
biblical_def: Prime is the first of the four “little hours”, said at about six in the morning as the house turned from the night office to the day's labour. Its office was brief: a hymn, a psalm portion, a short lesson, and in many houses the reading of the day's work assignments. It is the hour at which the monastic ideal shows itself most honestly, because it stands at the joint between prayer and work and refuses to separate them. Scripture sets the day's first business in the same place: “My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD” (Psa 5:3), and Christ himself “in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed” (Mar 1:35). The labour that followed was not a lesser thing: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10). Where prime went wrong was in the direction all the hours went wrong — recited at speed, often privately, counted as rendered. But the structure it embodied, that a man commits his work to God before he begins it, is not monastic property. It is ordinary Christian wisdom, and most households have lost it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines prime as the first canonical hour succeeding to lauds, and also the dawn or first appearance of light; first as advanced before all others in time; and work as labor, employment, or that which is produced by labor.
webster_full: PRIME, n. In the Romish church, the first canonical hour, succeeding to lauds.
PRIME, n. The dawn; the first appearance of light in the morning; hence, the beginning, the earliest stage.
PRIME, a. First in order of time; original; as, prime cost.
FIRST, a. Advanced before or further than any other in progression; foremost in place; preceding all others in time.
WORK, n. Labor; employment; exertion of strength, especially of manual strength; also, that which is produced by mental or physical labor.
scriptures: My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up.
And in the morning, rising up a great while before day, he went out, and departed into a solitary place, and there prayed.
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
corruption_summary: The first working hour of the monastic day: prayer set at the joint with labour, a structure now admired as a technique and seldom kept as a devotion.
corruption_paragraphs: The medieval defect was the common one — an hour recited rather than prayed, and credited as service rendered. Paul's correction is not to abolish the structure but to re-aim the labour it introduces: “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23). Work offered to God needs no cloister to make it holy, and no recited hour can make it holy if it is not so offered.

The modern misuse takes prime as a morning routine. The structure of a fixed early hour is genuinely useful and is now marketed on that basis alone, which empties it: a routine optimises the self, while prime committed the day to God. The principle to recover is the order of the two — address God first, then go to the work: “in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up” (Psa 5:3).
roots_summary: Latin primus, first; Hebrew boqer (H1242), morning; Hebrew abodah (H5656), labour or service; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Greek protos (G4413), first.
roots_lines: Latin primus — first; the hour named simply for standing first in the working day.
Hebrew boqer (H1242) — morning, daybreak; the hour's own setting.
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — labour, and also the service of worship; one Hebrew word covers both, which is prime's whole point.
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work or deed; “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Col 3:23).
Greek protos (G4413) — first in order or rank, the New Testament counterpart of primus.
usage: “rising up a great while before day” (Mar 1:35) — the Lord's own early hour, kept without a bell.
“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the labour prime sent the brethren out to.
“in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee” (Psa 5:3) — the day's first address, which is what the hour was for.

pos: n. (the second little hour, said at the third hour of the day, about nine in the morning)
etymology: Latin tertia hora, the third hour; from tertius, third. Also written tierce.
biblical_def: Terce is the office of the third hour, about nine in the morning by the Jewish reckoning Scripture uses. Of all the little hours it has the strongest New Testament association, for the third hour is when the Spirit fell at Pentecost — Peter answered the charge of drunkenness by pointing to the clock, and the church has prayed at that hour in memory of it ever since. The hour's hymn in the Roman use is a prayer for the Spirit, which is a sound instinct rightly grounded. The third hour is also the hour of the crucifixion in Mark's reckoning. Scripture itself, however, attaches no obligation to the hour, and the honest Protestant judgment on terce is twofold. The commemorative instinct is good: a church that remembers Pentecost daily is not thereby superstitious, and “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud” (Psa 55:17) shows the Psalmist dividing his day much the same way. The error was to make the commemoration a required work, and to let a recited Latin office stand in for the thing commemorated. The Spirit is sought by asking, not by keeping an anniversary.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives tierce as a third, and in liturgical use the third of the lesser hours; third as the ordinal of three; and defines hour as the twenty-fourth part of the natural day, with Pentecost as the feast of the fiftieth day.
webster_full: TIERCE, n. A third; the third of something. In the Romish breviary, one of the lesser hours of the office, said at the third hour of the day.
THIRD, a. The first after the second; the ordinal of three.
HOUR, n. A space of time equal to the twenty fourth part of the natural day.
PENTECOST, n. A solemn festival of the Jews, so called because celebrated on the fiftieth day after the sixteenth of Nisan; also, Whitsuntide, a festival of the christian church.
SPIRIT, n. In a theological sense, the Holy Spirit, the third person in the Trinity; also, an inspired or influencing power.
scriptures: Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.
Now Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.
And he spake a parable unto them to this end, that men ought always to pray, and not to faint;
On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:
corruption_summary: The third-hour office, kept in memory of Pentecost: a good commemoration turned into an owed recitation, and the Spirit sought by anniversary rather than by asking.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that remembering what God did at an hour is wholesome, while crediting the remembrance as a work is not. The hour itself commends nothing; the asking does: “men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1).

Terce also shows the real cost of an office said in a language the sayer does not command. An hour appointed to seek the Spirit, recited by rote in Latin by a brother who could not construe it, is the exact case Paul reasons about when he insists that the understanding must be engaged in prayer and praise. The Reformers' demand for the vernacular was not a concession to taste; it was the recovery of a hour's whole purpose.
roots_summary: Latin tertius, third; Greek hora (G5610), an hour; Greek pneuma (G4151), spirit; Greek pentekoste (G4005), the fiftieth; Hebrew shalosh (H7969), three.
roots_lines: Latin tertius — third; the hour named for its place in the day.
Greek hora (G5610) — an hour; “to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9) shows the same reckoning one hour on.
Greek pneuma (G4151) — spirit, breath, wind; the Person the hour's hymn addresses.
Greek pentekoste (G4005) — the fiftieth, the feast at whose third hour the Spirit was poured out.
Hebrew shalosh (H7969) — three; behind the Psalmist's threefold day of prayer.
usage: “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray” (Psa 55:17) — the threefold division the little hours elaborate.
“the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour” (Act 3:1) — apostolic practice marking hours without binding them.
“men ought always to pray, and not to faint” (Luk 18:1) — the standing duty no hour discharges.

pos: n. (the third little hour, said at the sixth hour of the day, about noon)
etymology: Latin sexta hora, the sixth hour; from sextus, sixth. The midday office.
biblical_def: Sext is the noon office, the sixth hour of the Jewish day. It has the clearest narrative warrant of any of the little hours, for it is at the sixth hour that Peter went up to pray and received the vision that opened the gospel to the Gentiles: “Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9). The Psalmist keeps the same hour — “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice” (Psa 55:17) — and it is the hour at which darkness covered the land at the crucifixion. Noon is also, practically, the hour at which a working man most needs recalling to God, which is why the monastic rule set an office there and why the loss of it is felt. The abuse of sext was not in its placement but in its accounting. An office owed at noon, hurried through so the meal might follow, is a transaction. The hour is worth keeping and worth keeping honestly: a man who stops at midday to pray is doing something Peter did, and something the Psalmist did, and he is doing it under no obligation but love.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) gives sext as the sixth of the canonical hours; sixth as the ordinal of six; noon as the middle of the day, or twelve o'clock; and midday as the middle of the day, noon.
webster_full: SEXT, n. In the Romish church, the sixth of the canonical hours, said at midday.
SIXTH, a. The first after the fifth; the ordinal of six.
NOON, n. The middle of the day; the time when the sun is in the meridian; twelve o'clock.
MIDDAY, n. The middle of the day; noon. Also used adjectively, as the midday sun.
HOUSETOP, n. The top or roof of a house; in the East, a flat place of resort for air, prayer or conversation.
scriptures: On the morrow, as they went on their journey, and drew nigh unto the city, Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour:
Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.
Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
corruption_summary: The noon office: the hour of Peter's housetop vision, kept by rule, and now the one hour of the day a working man reliably surrenders to his labour.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the pause itself. Noon is the hour most completely annexed by work in modern life, and the loss is not neutral — “Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17) is not kept by a man who never once lifts his head between breakfast and evening.

Where sext was corrupted, it was by haste: an office owed before the meal and dispatched to reach it. The remedy is not a longer office but a truer one. “Let my prayer be set forth before thee as incense; and the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice” (Psa 141:2) — prayer figured as a sacrifice is prayer that costs the man something, at noon as at evening.
roots_summary: Latin sextus, sixth; Hebrew tsohar (H6672), noon or midday; Greek hekto from hektos (G1623), sixth; Greek proseuchomai (G4336), to pray; Hebrew qetoreth (H7004), incense.
roots_lines: Latin sextus — sixth; the hour named for its place in the day.
Hebrew tsohar (H6672) — noon, the double light of midday; the Psalmist's “noon”.
Greek hektos (G1623) — sixth; “about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9).
Greek proseuchomai (G4336) — to pray, to address God; the verb of Peter's housetop.
Hebrew qetoreth (H7004) — incense; the figure under which prayer ascends.
usage: “Peter went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour” (Act 10:9) — the noon hour that opened the door to the Gentiles.
“and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice” (Psa 55:17) — midday prayer with the promise attached.
“Pray without ceasing” (1Th 5:17) — the rule that makes a noon office reasonable and a noon office insufficient.

pos: n. (the last office of the day, said before sleep, completing the round of hours)
etymology: Latin completorium, that which completes; from complere, to fill up or finish. The hour that completes the day.
biblical_def: Compline is the last office of the monastic day, said after supper and immediately before sleep, and it is the most humane of the hours. Its materials are the psalms of nightfall and committal, its prayers ask protection through the dark, and in most uses it ends with the brethren going to the dormitory in silence. The instinct is thoroughly biblical. “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety” (Psa 4:8) is compline in a sentence; so is “When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches” (Psa 63:6). Nor is the hour's realism about the night a medieval morbidity: Scripture itself treats sleep as a daily rehearsal of death and a daily exercise of trust. The defect of compline, where it had one, was not in its theology but in its company — the examination of conscience that closed it could drift into the treadmill of a merit account rather than rest in a finished atonement. Kept rightly, it remains the best of the hours for a Protestant to learn from: a day ended by committing body and soul to God, and then sleeping.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines compline as the last division of the Roman Catholic breviary and the last prayer at night; complete as having no deficiency, finished; and sleep as that state in which the voluntary functions are suspended.
webster_full: COMPLINE, n. The last division of the Roman Catholic breviary; the last prayer at night, to be recited after sun-set.
COMPLETE, a. Having no deficiency; perfect; finished; ended; concluded.
COMPLETE, v.t. To finish; to end; to perfect; to accomplish.
SLEEP, n. That state of an animal in which the voluntary exertion of his mental and corporeal powers is suspended, and he rests unconscious of what passes around him.
NIGHT, n. That part of the natural day when the sun is beneath the horizon, or the time from sunset to sunrise.
scriptures: I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep: for thou, LORD, only makest me dwell in safety.
When I remember thee upon my bed, and meditate on thee in the night watches.
It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep.
Yet the LORD will command his lovingkindness in the daytime, and in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life.
corruption_summary: The night office before sleep: the most humane of the hours, and the one whose closing self-examination could slide from repentance into a merit ledger.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sleep is an act of trust and ought to be entered as one. “It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2) rebukes the sleepless striver more sharply than any modern counsel does.

The live danger in a nightly examination of conscience is to audit the day against a standard one then tries to satisfy. That is the merit ledger, and it never balances. The examination is right; its resolution must be the blood of Christ and not tomorrow's amendment. “in the night his song shall be with me, and my prayer unto the God of my life” (Psa 42:8) — a song, not an accounting.
roots_summary: Latin completorium, the completing hour; Hebrew shakab (H7901), to lie down; Hebrew yashen (H3462), to sleep; Hebrew ashmurah (H821), a night watch; Greek hupnos (G5258), sleep.
roots_lines: Latin completorium — the hour that completes; from complere, to fill full.
Hebrew shakab (H7901) — to lie down; “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep” (Psa 4:8).
Hebrew ashmurah (H821) — a watch of the night; “meditate on thee in the night watches” (Psa 63:6).
Hebrew yashen (H3462) — to sleep; “so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2).
Greek hupnos (G5258) — sleep, both the natural rest and the figure of spiritual torpor.
usage: “I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep” (Psa 4:8) — compline reduced to its one necessary sentence.
“When I remember thee upon my bed” (Psa 63:6) — the night office of a man with no bell to call him.
“so he giveth his beloved sleep” (Psa 127:2) — the gift the hour was built to receive.

pos: n. pl. (the night office, the divisions of psalmody sung in the dark before dawn)
etymology: Latin nocturnus, of the night, from nox, night. The offices sung while it is still dark.
biblical_def: Nocturns are the night office: the two or three divisions of psalmody, lesson and responsory sung in the dark, in most uses beginning about two in the morning and running into matins and lauds at daybreak. No part of the monastic day cost more, and none has a plainer biblical anchor. “Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1) is a night office in one verse; “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee because of thy righteous judgments” (Psa 119:62) is the practice stated as a resolve; Paul and Silas sang at midnight in a prison. “Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord” (Lam 2:19) makes it a summons. The night office is therefore not a monastic peculiarity but a biblical pattern the monasteries institutionalised, and in institutionalising it they both preserved and damaged it: preserved, because the Psalter was sung through in the dark for a thousand years; damaged, because a rising owed at two in the morning becomes a discipline endured, and the rule had to legislate against brethren sleeping through it.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines nocturn as an office of devotion or religious service by night; nocturnal as pertaining to night; and watch as the division of the night, or the act of keeping awake for observation.
webster_full: NOCTURN, n. An office of devotion, or religious service by night.
NOCTURNAL, a. Pertaining to night; as nocturnal darkness. Also, done or happening by night, as a nocturnal expedition.
WATCH, n. The division of the night, as the first, second or third watch; also, forbearance of sleep, or the act of keeping awake.
VIGIL, n. Watch; devotion performed in the customary hours of rest or sleep; also, the eve or day preceding a church festival.
MIDNIGHT, n. The middle of the night; twelve o'clock at night. Used adjectively, as midnight studies.
scriptures: A Song of degrees. Behold, bless ye the LORD, all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD.
At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee because of thy righteous judgments.

Arise, cry out in the night: in the beginning of the watches pour out thine heart like water before the face of the Lord: lift up thy hands toward him for the life of thy young children, that faint for hunger in the top of every street.
I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search.
corruption_summary: The night office in the dark: the costliest of the hours, with the plainest warrant and the plainest temptation — a rising endured rather than offered.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the night is a fit time for prayer and the modern Christian has almost wholly abandoned it. “I call to remembrance my song in the night: I commune with mine own heart: and my spirit made diligent search” (Psa 77:6) describes an exercise few now attempt.

The historic defect was that obligation and sleep fought each other, and the rule had to adjudicate. An hour a man must rise to, under penalty, will sooner or later be risen to resentfully, and the Psalmist's night watch was never that. “in the night his song shall be with me” (Psa 42:8) — a song in the night comes from gladness, and no rule has ever been able to command it.
roots_summary: Latin nox, night; Hebrew layil (H3915), night; Hebrew ashmoreth (H821), a watch; Greek nux (G3571), night; Greek agrupnia (G70), sleeplessness or watching.
roots_lines: Latin nox, nocturnus — night, of the night; the hour's name and its whole character.
Hebrew layil (H3915) — night; “which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1).
Hebrew ashmoreth (H821) — a watch of the night; “in the beginning of the watches” (Lam 2:19).
Greek nux (G3571) — night; the hour of Paul and Silas singing in the Philippian jail.
Greek agrupnia (G70) — watchings, sleeplessness; Paul lists it among his sufferings, not his merits.
usage: “At midnight I will rise to give thanks unto thee” (Psa 119:62) — the night office in the Psalmist's own words.
“Arise, cry out in the night” (Lam 2:19) — the summons the monasteries obeyed more literally than we do.
“all ye servants of the LORD, which by night stand in the house of the LORD” (Psa 134:1) — a whole order of worship in one verse.

pos: n. (Latin, the work of God: Benedict's name for the daily office, to which nothing is to be preferred)
etymology: Latin opus, work, and Dei, of God: the work of God. In the Rule of Benedict, the name for the recited office.
biblical_def: Opus Dei — the Work of God — is Benedict's term for the daily office, and his rule lays down that nothing whatever is to be preferred to it. The phrase repays attention, because everything right and everything wrong about the monastic ideal is contained in it. What is right is the conviction that worship is work: real exertion, owed to God, taking precedence over the business men call urgent. Scripture agrees that worship is a labour and a sacrifice — “let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually” (Heb 13:15) — and that it is to be rendered in order and not at whim: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40). What is wrong is the drift the phrase invites. If the office is the work of God, then the labour of the kitchen, the field and the household becomes a lesser thing, and the man who prays professionally becomes a higher kind of Christian. Scripture will not have it. “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men” (Col 3:23) levels the ground: the plough is as much God's work as the psalm.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines work as labor, employment, and that which is produced by labor; opus is Latin for a work; and Webster defines divine service as the performance of duty to God in acts of worship.
webster_full: WORK, n. Labor; employment; exertion of strength; also, that which is made or done; a performance.
WORK, v.t. To labor; to be employed in performing; to toil; to exert strength in the accomplishment of a thing.
SERVICE, n. The performance of duty to God, in acts of worship; also, the office or duty of a servant.
OPUS, n. [L.] A work; used chiefly in composition and in the titles of works.
PREFER, v.t. To regard more than another; to honor or esteem above another; to choose or select in preference.
scriptures: By him therefore let us offer the sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of our lips giving thanks to his name.
Let all things be done decently and in order.
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men;
For even when we were with you, this we commanded you, that if any would not work, neither should he eat.
corruption_summary: Benedict's name for the recited office, “nothing preferred” to it: a high view of worship that quietly demoted every other kind of work.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption here is a real one and it is doctrinal, not merely devotional. To name the office the work of God is to create two tiers of Christian: those whose labour is worship and those whose labour is merely labour. From that distinction grew the whole apparatus of a religious estate, of prayers said for other men by professionals, and at last of merit transferred. Paul's correction is blunt: “if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10), and he wrote it to a congregation, not a cloister.

The principle to recover is the dignity of ordinary labour under God. A mother's work and a mason's are God's work; so is the psalm; and no one of them purchases anything. “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord” (Col 3:23) is the whole doctrine of vocation in a clause, and it dissolves the two tiers without despising the office that Benedict loved.
roots_summary: Latin opus Dei, the work of God; Hebrew abodah (H5656), labour and worship alike; Hebrew melakah (H4399), work or occupation; Greek ergon (G2041), a work; Greek leitourgia (G3009), service rendered.
roots_lines: Latin opus Dei — the work of God; Benedict's title for the office, and the hinge of the argument about it.
Hebrew abodah (H5656) — service, whether field labour or temple worship; Hebrew does not divide them.
Hebrew melakah (H4399) — work, occupation, business; the ordinary labour the Sabbath suspends.
Greek ergon (G2041) — a work or deed; “whatsoever ye do, do it heartily” (Col 3:23).
Greek leitourgia (G3009) — a public service; used of temple ministry and of a collection for the poor alike.
usage: “Let all things be done decently and in order” (1Co 14:40) — the warrant for an ordered office, and its limit.
“the sacrifice of praise to God continually” (Heb 13:15) — worship as real labour, which Benedict saw clearly.
“if any would not work, neither should he eat” (2Th 3:10) — the apostolic brake on a religion of professional prayer.

pos: n. (the service book containing the antiphons, responsories and chants of the daily office)
etymology: Greek antiphonos, sounding in answer, from anti, against or in return, and phone, a voice; through Latin antiphonarium, the book of answering chants.
biblical_def: The antiphonary is the choir book of the daily office: the volume holding the antiphons, responsories, invitatories and versicles with their chant, as distinct from the breviary which holds the text a man recites. Its organising principle is answer — one side of the choir sings, the other sings back — and that principle is biblical before it is monastic. Israel sang responsively at the sea and at the dedication of the wall; the Psalms are built for it, with their refrains and their paired lines; and the New Testament church is told to do something very like it: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord” (Eph 5:19), and “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16). Antiphonal singing is congregational teaching: each half of the choir hears the other confess the faith. The antiphonaries are also, incidentally, why we have the music at all — the great illuminated chant books of the abbeys preserved a repertory that would otherwise have vanished. Their defect was the defect of the whole system: Latin, and therefore sung over the heads of the people whose faith it confessed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines antiphonary as a service book containing the invitatories, responsories, collects and whatever is sung in the choir; antiphon as the answer of one choir to another; and chant as a song, or to sing in the cathedral manner.
webster_full: ANTIPHONARY, n. A service book, in Catholic countries, containing all the invitatories, responsories, versicles, collects, and whatever is sung in the choir, except the lessons.
ANTIPHON, n. The answer of one choir to another, when a psalm or anthem is sung by two choirs; also, a species of psalmody.
ANTIPHONAL, a. Pertaining to antiphons or alternate singing.
CHANT, v.t. To sing; to utter with a melodious voice; also, to sing after the manner of a cathedral service.
RESPONSORY, n. The answer of the people to the priest in alternate speaking; also, an anthem sung after a lesson.
scriptures: Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody in your heart to the Lord;
Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.
O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever.
Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.
corruption_summary: The choir book of answering chants: antiphonal praise is biblical and congregational, and a Latin antiphonary sang it over the people's heads.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that praise is meant to be answered and not merely received. “O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever” (Psa 136:1) is built for two voices, and a congregation that only ever listens has lost something the abbeys at least retained.

The real defect of the antiphonaries was linguistic, and it is a sobering one for any church fond of its own music. A faith confessed antiphonally in a tongue the people do not know is a confession made past them. Paul's rule for the assembly is that singing instructs — “teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Col 3:16) — and whatever cannot teach, however beautiful, has failed at the thing it was for.
roots_summary: Greek antiphonos, sounding in answer; Greek phone (G5456), a voice; Hebrew anah (H6030), to answer or respond in song; Hebrew shir (H7892), a song; Greek psalmos (G5568), a psalm.
roots_lines: Greek anti and phone (G5456) — voice in return; the answering that names the book.
Hebrew anah (H6030) — to answer, and so to sing responsively; the verb of Miriam answering Moses at the sea.
Hebrew shir (H7892) — a song; the Psalter's own word for what the choir carries.
Greek psalmos (G5568) — a psalm, a song struck on strings; “psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19).
Greek ode (G5603) — an ode or song; the third term of Paul's triad, and the broadest of them.
usage: “Speaking to yourselves in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs” (Eph 5:19) — the apostolic warrant for answering praise.
“teaching and admonishing one another in psalms” (Col 3:16) — singing as instruction, which is why the tongue matters.
“Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD” (Psa 150:6) — the antiphon no choir book is large enough to hold.
